meta.run_summary: First run. 64 articles read, 59 passed the thermal check, grouped into 25 opportunities across the three areas.

coverage.datacentre: Good coverage of cold plates and heat reuse. Few UK chip-level companies found so far.
coverage.aerospace: Strong on oil coolers and hydrogen. Little news on cabin-air precoolers specifically, so the daily run will keep looking (Liebherr, Collins, Honeywell, ATI).
coverage.motorsport: Teams publish little, so most evidence comes from suppliers (Conflux, PWR, Constellium). Henry's steer here will help most.

cards.headline: Light air radiators for megawatt fuel-cell aircraft, which FlyZero calls a UK opportunity
cards.problem: Fuel-cell aircraft must reject megawatts of low-grade heat (stacks at about 80 C), and radiators can dominate weight and drag.
cards.technology: Compact air radiators: microtube, TPMS lattice and printed cores, targeting 5 to over 20 kW/kg.
cards.why: FlyZero names fuel-cell air radiators as the biggest thermal challenge for hydrogen aircraft, and its UK capability report calls 'novel air radiator heat exchangers with a commercially attractive manufacturing method' a high-opportunity area for the UK. Several designs compete: Reaction Engines' microtube radiator on Project FRESSON (claimed over 300 kW), DLR's printed TPMS exchangers (TRL 4) and Conflux's printed exchanger for Airbus ZEROe. That FlyZero phrase reads almost like an MTC mission statement.

applicability.reason: All sources target fuel-cell aircraft thermal management.

trl.reason: DLR at TRL 4; FlyZero puts the global best at TRL 5 on a rig.

cards.barriers: Target kW/kg is far above today's radiators, and hydrogen aircraft timelines keep slipping.
cards.next_step: Talk to Cranfield Aerospace Solutions about what FRESSON's radiator relies on now that Reaction Engines is in administration.

cards.headline: Printed compact air-oil coolers for geared ultra-high-bypass engines
cards.problem: Geared and UHBR turbofans reject more oil heat, with less space for coolers and a fuel-burn penalty for every bit of drag.
cards.technology: Additively manufactured compact air-oil heat exchangers, including curved coolers that conform to the engine.
cards.why: This is the oil-cooler brief exactly, and the UK is strong in it. Meggitt (now Parker Meggitt) and TWI ran C-ALM AOHE to build an 80 kW, under-10 kg printed air-oil cooler for geared UHBR engines, aiming at TRL 6 and MRL 6, and published a review of L-PBF aluminium heat exchangers with Birmingham. Safran's HIPEX shows the payoff: a printed curved cooler, claimed to halve drag and save up to 1% fuel, already ground-tested on an engine.

applicability.reason: Both projects target turbofan oil cooling.

trl.reason: C-ALM targeted TRL 6; HIPEX has completed engine ground tests.

cards.barriers: Flight certification of printed aluminium heat exchangers; fatigue and fouling data; powder removal from fine fins.
cards.next_step: Ask TWI and Parker Meggitt what limited C-ALM's final TRL and MRL, and whether inspecting internal passages was the blocker. MTC metrology could fill that gap.

cards.headline: 3D-printed passive two-phase evaporators that cool chips with no pumps or fans
cards.problem: Cooling energy in data centres and HPC (pumps, fans, chillers), and low-grade waste heat that is hard to reuse.
cards.technology: Passive two-phase thermosiphon evaporator (vapour chamber) printed as one aluminium part.
cards.why: DTI and Heatflow printed the evaporator in one piece by laser powder bed fusion, which removes joints and leak paths, and tested it at 600 W, 50% above target, with no pumps or fans. Heat leaves at 60-80 C, warm enough for district heating, which ties it to the UK heat-network push. It is still the clearest Venn centre found: the advance exists because of how the part is made.

applicability.reason: The project itself targets data-centre and HPC cooling.

trl.reason: Tested demonstrator at component level; no deployment yet.

cards.barriers: 600 W per device is below today's 1 kW+ GPUs; scale-up and long-term fluid compatibility of printed aluminium are unproven.
cards.next_step: Ask DTI about their PBF-LB parameters and leak testing for thin-wall two-phase parts. An RTO-to-RTO comparison of printed evaporator quality would be a natural first conversation.

cards.headline: Fine-feature copper cold plates matched to each chip's heat map
cards.problem: AI chips above 1 kW, in racks heading for 600 kW, outgrow machined microchannel cold plates.
cards.technology: Copper cold plates with 30-70 micron features concentrated where the chip runs hottest.
cards.why: Three start-ups reach the same goal by different routes. Fabric8Labs prints copper electrochemically at 33 microns, Corintis designs microchannels in software and makes them at volume (in a Microsoft test, three times better heat removal), and Alloy Enterprises laser-cuts copper sheets and diffusion bonds them. MTC covers both the additive and the laser routes, so it could benchmark them fairly. The Microsoft result is the only independent number.

applicability.reason: All three companies sell into AI data-centre cooling.

trl.reason: Corintis has shipped over 10,000 plates and Fabric8Labs is in Wiwynn products; Alloy is earlier.

cards.barriers: Cost per plate against skived and machined copper, and proving no fouling or leaks over years of service.
cards.next_step: Corintis is the most mature and is in Switzerland. Ask what limits their volume route, and whether they want an independent test partner in Europe.

cards.headline: Configurable printed oil coolers, proven in an endurance race
cards.problem: Teams need custom heat exchangers quickly, inside a fixed envelope.
cards.technology: Parametric (configurable) printed heat-exchanger cores.
cards.why: A Conflux transmission oil cooler, built in two weeks on its configurable core platform, finished a full endurance race on a Multimatic car with about 20% more heat rejection than the incumbent in the same space and no added weight. Configurable cores turn heat-exchanger design into choosing parameters, which shortens lead times and suits low-volume work in both motorsport and aerospace. Conflux also works with Dallara and is opening a UK hub.

applicability.reason: Race-proven in motorsport.

trl.reason: Completed a full endurance race.

cards.barriers: Cost per part, and only one published race result.
cards.next_step: Ask Conflux's UK hub whether the configurable platform has been tried for aerospace oil coolers.

cards.headline: The UK's compact aero-engine heat exchanger programme, with MTC already a partner
cards.problem: Next-generation passenger engines need lighter, more compact heat exchangers.
cards.technology: Compact heat-exchanger design and manufacturing development, plus ducted installations validated in a full-scale wind tunnel.
cards.why: An ATI-funded £7.4m programme runs from Meggitt's Midlands Thermal Management Centre of Excellence with AMRC, AFRC, the MTC, S&C Thermal Fluids and Cranfield. A related ATI case study (DBAHX, £0.87m) shows Parker Meggitt validating a ducted heat exchanger in a full-scale wind tunnel with a printed ejector. MTC is already inside this, so the roadmap value is knowing what was learnt and who at MTC holds it. S&C Thermal Fluids is a small UK firm worth knowing.

applicability.reason: The programme targets aero-engine heat exchangers.

trl.reason: Wind-tunnel validation for DBAHX; programme results not public.

cards.barriers: Results are not public and the IP sits with Parker Meggitt.
cards.next_step: Start inside MTC: find who worked on this programme, then ask Parker Meggitt about the next phase.

cards.headline: Designing liquid cooling for total energy, pump work included: an F1 lesson
cards.problem: Liquid-cooling energy is dominated by pumping across thousands of cold plates, not by the cold plates' heat transfer.
cards.technology: Low-pressure-drop printed cold plates designed with CFD and system-level models.
cards.why: Conflux, led by a former F1 engineer, argues the right measure is thermal resistance per unit of pump power, and quotes 0.0076 C/W at 6 L/min for its printed plates. Henry rated this the best example in the calibration set. It is an opinion piece with one vendor number, which holds the evidence score back, but the motorsport-to-data-centre transfer is exactly the cross-area link the tool should surface. Conflux is opening a UK hub.

applicability.reason: The article is written for data-centre cooling buyers.

trl.reason: Conflux sells cold plates; the system-level claim is not independently tested.

cards.barriers: No independent comparison; buyers rarely specify pump energy at component level.
cards.next_step: Conflux's new UK hub is the easy route in. Ask whether they would share test data comparing pump power against a conventional plate.

cards.headline: Using cryogenic hydrogen fuel as the heat sink in a turbofan
cards.problem: Hydrogen gas turbines must heat fuel from -253 C to injection temperature, and can use that cold to cool the engine.
cards.technology: Fuel-to-oil, intercooler and recuperator heat exchangers with cryogenic hydrogen as the coolant.
cards.why: Chalmers and GKN reported almost 8% lower take-off fuel burn and 37% lower NOx by cooling engine parts with hydrogen and preheating it with exhaust heat. Oxford's £9.5m EPSRC programme, with Imperial and Loughborough and backed by Rolls-Royce, Airbus and Parker, is building heat-transfer data for cryogenic fuel lines. FlyZero rates cryogenic heat exchangers at TRL 3 globally, held back by materials data, sealing and test facilities, and says UK firms go to the US to test.

applicability.reason: All sources target hydrogen aero engines.

trl.reason: Rig tests and modelling; FlyZero puts the global state at TRL 3.

cards.barriers: No large UK cryogenic hydrogen test facility; little hydrogen-embrittlement data for printed alloys.
cards.next_step: The Oxford programme has industry supporters and studentships; ask whether it needs manufacturing partners for test articles.

cards.headline: Inspecting and qualifying printed heat exchangers: the gap FlyZero names
cards.problem: Printed heat exchangers cannot fly until internal passages, thin walls and joints can be inspected and lifed.
cards.technology: NDT and qualification of AM heat-exchanger cores: CT, leak testing, thin-wall property data, repeatable joints.
cards.why: FlyZero's roadmap lists the enablers for hydrogen heat exchangers and most are manufacturing problems: no thin-wall property data, bespoke assembly tooling, a need for automated NDT and repeatable joints, and qualification of AM materials from -253 C to 500 C. Its capability report says lifing printed heat exchangers is still a challenge, with HVM Catapult (MTC) and TWI studying AM and automated laser welding. The same gaps hold back printed oil coolers for today's engines, so the work pays off before hydrogen arrives.

applicability.reason: FlyZero states these gaps for hydrogen aircraft; that they also apply to today's oil coolers is our inference.

trl.reason: Gaps identified; no qualification route yet.

cards.barriers: Needs a programme sponsor; qualification data is slow and costly to generate.
cards.next_step: A strong candidate for MTC's own roadmap. Check whether the ATI has funded follow-up to these FlyZero gaps since 2022.

cards.headline: Racing-approved alloys and print parameters for thin-wall heat exchangers
cards.problem: Printed heat exchangers need alloys that stay strong when hot and print leak-tight at fine fin thickness.
cards.technology: Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) heat-exchanger alloy with qualified L-PBF parameter sets.
cards.why: Constellium's Aheadd CP1 was approved for F1 in 2023 and PWR has supplied printed heat exchangers in it since 2024. Eplus3D's parameters reach 99.93% density with leak-tight thin tube walls. This is the motorsport version of the aerospace qualification problem, already solved at racing scale. Parameter development and density and leak verification for heat-exchanger alloys is core MTC work, and the racing data could seed aerospace qualification.

applicability.reason: Approved and in use in F1.

trl.reason: In use in F1 since 2024.

cards.barriers: Aerospace material approval is a much higher bar; PWR and Constellium hold the know-how.
cards.next_step: Ask Constellium whether CP1 is being qualified for aerospace heat exchangers, and who is generating the data.

cards.headline: Megawatt-class thermal management for hybrid-electric regional aircraft
cards.problem: Hybrid-electric aircraft generate 300-1000 kW of waste heat, against 35-50 kW in similar aircraft today.
cards.technology: Air-cycle and vapour-cycle systems with printed air-to-air and air-to-liquid exchangers, developed with a digital twin.
cards.why: TheMa4HERA is a €33.5m Clean Aviation project led by Honeywell, aiming for TRL 5 in 2026 with a full-scale ground demonstrator at Fraunhofer. Conflux joined in 2025 to make printed exchangers, evaporators and condensers. The partner list (Liebherr, Collins, Calyos, DLR, NLR, plus UK partners Conflux UK, Honeywell UK and Element Digital Engineering) is a map of who matters in aircraft environmental control heat exchangers. Results are due around the end of 2026.

applicability.reason: The project targets aircraft thermal management.

trl.reason: TRL 5 target for 2026; flight tests planned from 2027.

cards.barriers: Hybrid-electric regional aircraft entry into service is uncertain.
cards.next_step: Watch for TheMa4HERA results at the end of 2026. Calyos, a small Belgian two-phase company in the consortium, may be worth a call.

cards.headline: F1's 2026 rules: more electric heat to reject, less air to do it
cards.problem: 2026 cars nearly triple MGU-K power to 350 kW while losing downforce and cooling airflow; active aero makes duct flow transient.
cards.technology: Low-temperature circuits for battery, MGU-K and electronics; non-rectangular heat exchangers; transient system models.
cards.why: Mercedes HPP says cooling must be designed into the aero concept from the start, and Modelon describes the shift from steady to transient thermal design as active aero changes duct flow. Oxford Brookes is modelling MGU-K heat losses under the new rules, and team sidepods show the result: tight wraps around heat exchangers and swappable cooling panels. The problem is clear; non-rectangular printed cores and transient models are where MTC fits.

applicability.reason: All sources are about F1's 2026 cooling.

trl.reason: The cars race; the new design methods are less mature.

cards.barriers: Teams keep their solutions secret, and the market is small though influential.
cards.next_step: Oxford Brookes' motorsport group is the most open route into this problem.

cards.headline: Printed heat exchangers for aircraft air systems and precoolers
cards.problem: Bleed-air precoolers and environmental control heat exchangers are brazed plate-fin assemblies with many joints, shaped by the space they must fit.
cards.technology: AM heat-exchanger cores with fewer joints and shapes fitted to the installation; software-generated precooler surfaces.
cards.why: Liebherr Aerospace, Europe's leading air-systems supplier, set the topic for NATHENA, a Clean Sky 2 project that built a scale-one printed aircraft heat exchanger with fewer welded and brazed parts and a shape fitted to the aircraft. LEAP 71 and Farsoon have since printed a 1.5 m precooler in one piece with software-generated surfaces, though it is a hypersonic concept with no data. This is the closest match yet to the precooler brief, and also the main coverage gap.

applicability.reason: NATHENA targets civil aircraft heat exchangers; LEAP 71's precooler is for hypersonic, not turbofan, use.

trl.reason: Lab-tested proof of concept (NATHENA) and a concept print (LEAP 71).

cards.barriers: Brazed plate-fin precoolers are mature and cheap, so printed ones must win on weight or installation to justify qualification.
cards.next_step: Ask Liebherr Toulouse what happened after NATHENA and whether printed precoolers are on its roadmap.

cards.headline: Printed battery cold plates, CT-checked, in a 2026 F1 power unit
cards.problem: 2026 power units carry much larger batteries and electronics; Honda says battery and motor thermal management will decide reliability.
cards.technology: AM battery cold plates and cooling plates with CT-based inspection.
cards.why: Ford has made around 1,000 printed parts for the 2026 Red Bull Ford power unit, including battery cold plates, and each one goes through strength tests, 3D scanning, X-ray and CT before metrology. Honda says battery and motor thermal management is where manufacturers will differ. Inspection at that rate is familiar MTC ground, and these cold plates are close cousins of data-centre ones.

applicability.reason: Both sources are about 2026 F1 power units.

trl.reason: Racing in 2026.

cards.barriers: Team-confidential; little public data.

sources.title: Additively manufactured parts testing underway for 2026 Ford and Red Bull F1 debut

cards.headline: UK cooling money goes to facilities, not to chip-level cooling
cards.problem: UK cooling investment is concentrated in two firms, and chip-level cooling, where manufacturing matters most, has only one UK company named.
cards.technology: Chip-level cold plates and two-phase cooling.
cards.why: Tracxn counts $362m raised by UK cooling and heat-reuse firms, second only to the US, but almost all of it went to Deep Green and Iceotope, and it names one UK chip-level company, Infiniflux. Chip level is where printed and laser-made parts give the biggest gains (see the cold-plate cards). A thin UK supply base is a reason for an RTO to help, and a reason to call Infiniflux.

applicability.reason: The report is about investment; the link to MTC manufacturing support is our inference.

trl.reason: Market signal, not a technology.

cards.barriers: The UK market for chip-level parts is small and US and Swiss start-ups are ahead.
cards.next_step: Find out what Infiniflux makes and whether it needs manufacturing help.

cards.headline: GPU simulation cuts heat-exchanger design from months to two weeks
cards.problem: Heat-exchanger design and validation loops take months, which limits how many variants get tried.
cards.technology: GPU-accelerated conjugate heat-transfer CFD combined with implicit modelling.
cards.why: Sintavia ran a 30-million-cell conjugate heat-transfer model in seven minutes on Nvidia GPUs, 11 times faster than on CPUs, and designed a multi-circuit heat exchanger in two weeks. It claims 30% less weight and 20% better thermal efficiency, checked by CT scanning. Faster simulation means many variants a week instead of one a month, and MTC's modelling team could test whether the workflow holds for its own work. The gains are company claims.

applicability.reason: The heat exchanger is for aerospace.

trl.reason: Designed, printed and CT-checked; no published test data.

cards.barriers: Vendor claims; commercial CFD licensing on GPUs.

sources.title: Multi-circuit aerospace heat exchanger designed in 'record time'

cards.headline: Gyroid-core fuel-cooled oil coolers designed for printing
cards.problem: Fuel-cooled oil coolers must pass more heat in less volume while keeping fuel above icing temperature.
cards.technology: TPMS (gyroid) heat-exchanger cores designed with implicit modelling and CFD.
cards.why: nTop and Ansys show a full design workflow for a printed gyroid fuel-cooled oil cooler, based on an America Makes project, and Honeywell was testing printed fuel-oil exchangers as early as 2015. The design tools are now commodity. What is missing is test data showing gyroid cores beat plate-fin designs once pressure drop, fouling and inspection are counted, which is a build-and-test job.

applicability.reason: The workflow targets aero-engine fuel-oil cooling.

trl.reason: Design and simulation; no published test data.

cards.barriers: Fuel-side fouling and cleaning of TPMS passages.

sources.title: Unlocking Advanced Heat Exchanger Design and Simulation with nTop Platform and ANSYS CFX
Honeywell to Test Printed Heat Exchanger

cards.headline: Software that grows cold-plate channels for one specific chip
cards.problem: Hot spots on large AI packages such as the Nvidia GB200 set the peak temperature and limit performance.
cards.technology: Generative (reaction-diffusion) channel design coupled to a thermal model.
cards.why: University of Michigan-Dearborn's simulation cut peak temperature by over 35 C against a parallel-channel plate. It is simulation only, and the shapes would need printing or fine machining. That is the gap MTC can fill: design for manufacture, build, and test whether the gain survives real tolerances and surface finish. This is the kind of paper the old tool missed because the manufacturing link is implicit.

applicability.reason: The paper targets the GB200 directly; the manufacturing route is our inference.

trl.reason: Simulation only, no prototype.

cards.barriers: Simulated gains often shrink once minimum wall thickness, powder removal and roughness are applied.
cards.next_step: A small MTC study: print the generated geometry and a baseline, and measure the real difference.

sources.title: Generative Design for Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling for Data Centers

cards.headline: Printed brake ducts for faster development under new FIA limits
cards.problem: Brake discs over 700 C must be cooled within FIA duct rules, now with devices that heat or cool wheels and brakes banned.
cards.technology: Simulation-led brake-duct design with printed prototypes and carbon-PEEK race parts.
cards.why: Cadillac F1 prints brake-duct prototypes to check its simulations, and Visa Cash App RB prints race ducts in carbon-fibre PEEK on Roboze machines, cutting lead time by 66%. The FIA ban moves the job back to duct geometry. Polymer AM is mature here, so novelty is modest.

applicability.reason: All sources are about F1 brake cooling.

trl.reason: In use on race cars.

cards.barriers: Low novelty and well served by existing suppliers.

cards.headline: Sheffield's Iceotope scales sealed-chassis liquid cooling
cards.problem: Energy and water use of air-cooled data centres as AI racks densify.
cards.technology: Sealed-chassis precision immersion using a small volume of dielectric coolant.
cards.why: Iceotope holds over 200 patents, claims up to 40% lower energy and 96% lower water use, and raised a $26m Series B in May 2026 to scale its KUL AI racks. Its next challenge is making sealed chassis at volume, which is an assembly and manufacturing problem more than a physics one. It is a UK company close to MTC's patch, though the performance figures are its own.

applicability.reason: Iceotope sells data-centre cooling.

trl.reason: Products on sale; performance claims not independently verified.

cards.barriers: Dielectric fluid supply and PFAS rules; chassis must suit many server designs.
cards.next_step: Ask Iceotope where its production bottleneck is as it scales after the Series B.

cards.headline: Where the UK's microtube heat-exchanger know-how went after Reaction Engines
cards.problem: The UK's leading microtube precooler developer went into administration in October 2024.
cards.technology: Microtube precoolers and radiators (SABRE precooler, FRESSON fuel-cell radiator).
cards.why: Reaction Engines made very fine-tube heat exchangers that cooled hypersonic intake air, were used in F1 cooling and were chosen for the FRESSON fuel-cell radiator. Administrators were selling the IP in 2025 with a preferred bidder in exclusivity. FlyZero listed Reaction Engines as a UK strength, so where the IP and people went matters for UK capability. Joining and assembling thousands of microtubes is a joining and automation problem MTC knows.

applicability.reason: The sources are business news; the link to MTC joining and automation is our inference.

trl.reason: Precooler tested in 2019; radiator claimed for FRESSON.

cards.barriers: Unclear who owns the IP now.
cards.next_step: Find out who bought the IP; a new owner may be looking for manufacturing partners.

cards.headline: Getting data-centre heat into UK heat networks
cards.problem: UK data-centre growth (NESO: 35 TWh a year by 2050, about 40% for cooling) and the need to decarbonise heat.
cards.technology: Heat recovery at 25-40 C, raised to 55-80 C by heat pumps or by liquid cooling that runs hotter.
cards.why: Policy and money are lining up. DESNZ put £90m into heat networks fed by data centres, Deep Green has approval for a 5.6 MW site in Bradford, and EnergiRaven models enough heat for 3.5-6.3m homes by 2035. MTC's angle is upstream: the hotter the coolant leaves the chip, the less heat-pump work is needed, which favours two-phase and printed cold plates that run warm. Strong on UK relevance, weaker on a direct MTC role.

applicability.reason: None of these sources mention manufacturing; the link through hotter-running cold plates is ours.

trl.reason: Heat networks are mature; high-temperature chip cooling is not.

cards.barriers: Data centres are rarely near heat demand, and heat-supply contracts are slow.
cards.next_step: Watch the DESNZ-funded schemes for the coolant temperatures they specify.

cards.headline: Two-phase immersion cooling coupled straight into a heat pump
cards.problem: Reusing hyperscale (over 50 MW) data-centre heat at useful temperatures.
cards.technology: Two-phase immersion with the coolant condensing directly in a natural-refrigerant heat pump.
cards.why: SINTEF's CoolHeatDC removes the intermediate water loop by condensing the immersion fluid in the heat pump's evaporator, raising the temperature available for district heating. The condenser-evaporator is a compact two-phase heat exchanger, a good fit for printed designs, though SINTEF does not say so. Lab scale only so far.

applicability.reason: SINTEF targets data centres; the printed heat-exchanger angle is our inference.

trl.reason: Lab tests and techno-economic modelling.

cards.barriers: Two-phase dielectric fluids face PFAS restrictions in Europe.

sources.title: CoolHeatDC - Two-phase immersion cooling with integrated heat upgrade in data centres

cards.headline: Waterless two-phase direct-to-chip cooling for 4 kW processors
cards.problem: Next-generation processors above 4 kW and water scarcity at data-centre sites.
cards.technology: Two-phase evaporators mounted directly on the chip with a dielectric refrigerant.
cards.why: ZutaCore raised $100m from Mitsubishi Electric, Carrier and Samsung and is in over 75 sites. On-chip two-phase evaporators are where DTI's printed evaporator would compete, so this shows the market is real. Investment news with little technical detail.

applicability.reason: ZutaCore sells data-centre cooling.

trl.reason: Deployed commercially.

cards.barriers: Refrigerant choice under PFAS rules; servicing and leak detection.

sources.title: ZutaCore secures $100m Series C funding to push liquid cooling tech

cards.headline: Heatwaves and UK AI compute: is heat rejection sized for new summers?
cards.problem: UK heatwaves (37.3 C June 2026 record) push dry coolers and chillers past their design ambient.
cards.technology: Heat rejection sized for higher ambient, and liquid cooling that runs warmer.
cards.why: Cambridge's Dawn AI supercomputer went offline during the June 2026 heatwave. The cause was not confirmed as thermal, but it raises a UK-specific question about design ambient temperatures. A problem signal rather than a technology; worth watching for a confirmed cause.

applicability.reason: The article does not confirm a thermal cause; the heat-rejection link is our reading.

trl.reason: Problem signal.

cards.barriers: Cause unconfirmed.
